power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.191", "P = 0.159", "P = 0.200" ), Sentence = c("Relative to <4.0 mmol/L, the adjusted HR was 0.65 (95% CI, 0.52-0.83; P < 0.001) for 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L. The two remaining categories did not differ significantly from the reference: 0.88 (95% CI, 0.73-1.07; P = 0.191) for 4.0-<4.5 mmol/L and 0.80 (95% CI, 0.59-1.09; P = 0.159) for ≥5.0 mmol/L, the latter resting on 272 patients with 58 events.", "Relative to <4.0 mmol/L, the adjusted HR was 0.65 (95% CI, 0.52-0.83; P < 0.001) for 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L. text.text: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are standard therapy for primary aldosteronism (PA).
Serum potassium is measured in nearly every treated patient, but the long-term prognostic value of potassium attained early after initiation is undefined.
In the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with PA newly initiating spironolactone or eplerenone in 2000-2025, without prior adrenalectomy (n=4,169; 180-day landmark design).
Achieved potassium (last value on days 14-180) was categorised as <4.0, 4.0-<4.5, 4.5-<5.0 and ≥5.0 mmol/L, and its change from baseline in tertiles, using cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray models.

Primary aldosteronism (PA) is the most common endocrine cause of hypertension, and the cardiovascular risk it carries is not explained by blood pressure (BP) alone.

Compared with essential hypertension at similar BP, it is associated with higher risks of stroke (odds ratio 2.58, 95% CI 1.93-3.45), coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure (HF; odds ratio 2.05, 95% CI 1.11-3.78), 1 and that excess is not abolished by treatment: among patients treated with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), the adjusted hazard of incident cardiovascular events remains almost twice that of matched patients with essential hypertension. 2 Hypokalaemia, the feature that most often prompts testing, is present in only a minority of cases, 3 so potassium serves less as a diagnostic marker than as the parameter monitored in nearly every treated patient.

text.text: What constitutes an adequate response to medical treatment therefore has direct prognostic consequences, and it remains unsettled.

The Primary Aldosteronism Medical Treatment Outcome (PAMO) consensus defines a complete biochemical response as correction of hypokalaemia without potassium supplementation together with normalisation of renin, and found that only about half of medically treated patients achieve it. 4 Its potassium criterion, like the rest of the definition, was set by Delphi consensus: correction is defined as a serum potassium of at least 3.6 mmol/L, the same threshold used for biochemical success after adrenalectomy in the Primary Aldosteronism Surgical Outcome (PASO) consensus, 5 and one that has not, to our knowledge, been validated against cardiovascular outcomes.

text.text: Potassium occupies an unusual position in this framework.

A 2026 review ranks its normalisation second among the three objectives of medical therapy, while stating that no specific target level exists for PA. 11 The target levels that exist come from other populations, where the potassium-mortality relationship is U-shaped and lowest at about 4.0-4.5 mmol/L [11] [12] [13] [14] [15] -so a higher achieved concentration cannot be assumed to be better.

text.text: We therefore used a landmark design to examine whether the early potassium response to MRA therapy, expressed both as the achieved concentration and as the change from baseline, is associated with subsequent cardiovascular events and incident HF in adults with PA, whether such association is confined to the correction of frank hypokalaemia, and how it relates to the change in renin.

Data were obtained from the TriNetX Research Network, a federated electronic health record network providing de-identified clinical data from 91 contributing healthcare organisations, yielding 10,661 unique patients (10,077 after the diagnosis-code exclusions below).
Individual informed consent was waived under Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).

The case definition remains administrative, with no requirement for confirmatory testing: about half the analytic cohort carried a code specific to PA and most of the remainder only unspecified hyperaldosteronism.
We used a landmark design to separate measurement of the early biochemical response from the accrual of outcomes.
Baseline potassium was the last value in the 365 days before the index date; achieved potassium was the last value on days 14 to 180, and the landmark was day 180.
Follow-up was measured from the landmark, and events before it were exclusions rather than outcomes.
Achieved potassium was categorised as <4.0, 4.0 to <4.5, 4.5 to <5.0 and ≥5.0 mmol/L, with <4.0 as the reference; the change from baseline (ΔK) was analysed in tertiles.

The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke and all-cause death.
Incident HF was a co-primary outcome, analysed in the subset free of HF both at baseline and through the landmark.
Non-fatal outcomes were required to be coded at an inpatient, acute-care or emergency encounter, and follow-up continued until the outcome, death, or the last recorded encounter.

Because all-cause death contributes a substantial share of composite events and its ascertainment varies by calendar era in this network, we additionally report the composite restricted to myocardial infarction and stroke, and examine the association by calendar period of MRA initiation.

Models were adjusted for age, sex, race, MRA agent, baseline potassium, baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease (CKD), atrial fibrillation and ischemic heart disease, and for concomitant medications recorded from 180 days before the index date through the landmark: angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, thiazides, loop diuretics and potassium supplements.
Models were stratified on prevalent cerebrovascular disease (ICD-10 I60-I69) and, for the composite outcome, on prevalent HF. eGFR was estimated with the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation.

Race was categorised as recorded in the electronic health record (White, Black or African American, Asian, other or unknown) and was retained as a covariate because it was associated with both achieved potassium and outcome; models with and without race are compared in Supplementary Table S31.

text.text: ΔeGFR and achieved BP are measured in the exposure window and were therefore excluded from the primary models and examined in sensitivity analyses (S11, S34); all estimates are multivariable-adjusted associations rather than causal effects.
The proportional hazards assumption was assessed via scaled Schoenfeld residuals for every model term and an explicit interaction between exposure and a split of follow-up at three years.
Fine-Gray subdistribution models, treating death as a competing event, were fitted as a sensitivity analysis for incident HF.

Three-year cumulative incidence from the landmark was estimated unadjusted by the Aalen-Johansen estimator and, adjusted, by g-formula standardisation over the fitted model, with percentile confidence intervals from 500 nonparametric bootstrap replicates.

Departure from a linear dose-response was examined by nested likelihood-ratio tests comparing a linear term against fractional polynomials and restricted cubic splines, with and without a knot at 5.0 mmol/L; these are global tests of fit, not tests of where a departure lies.

text.text: In 4,169 adults with PA starting an MRA, the potassium concentration attained in the first six months was associated with subsequent cardiovascular risk, and the association was not a simple gradient.

text.text: A larger rise from baseline was associated with lower risk on a monotone gradient.
The band associated with the lowest risk lies inside the reference range, and the association persisted when frankly hypokalaemic patients were removed.
These findings bear directly on how medical treatment of PA is monitored.

Potassium is measured in nearly every treated patient, yet consensus criteria count correction of hypokalaemia, a potassium of at least 3.6 mmol/L, as an adequate response, 4 and guidance sets no potassium target beyond normalisation. 7, 11 In this cohort that threshold did not separate patients by subsequent risk, whereas risk was lowest in a band almost 1 mmol/L higher.

text.text: If confirmed, a potassium below 4.5 mmol/L under treatment would identify patients whose MRA dose, adherence or supplementation merits review, using a test that is already part of routine monitoring, and the potassium criterion in consensus definitions of treatment response would merit reconsideration.
These data do not show that raising potassium lowers risk; they define the target that a titration trial should test.
Several mechanisms, not mutually exclusive, could link the potassium attained under MRA therapy to subsequent risk.
The first treats potassium as a read-out of receptor blockade in the kidney.

Aldosterone acting through the mineralocorticoid receptor in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron increases sodium reabsorption through the epithelial sodium channel and, through the lumen-negative potential this generates, potassium secretion through ROMK and BK channels; 16 an MRA reverses both, so the rise in potassium after initiation indexes the extent to which renal receptor activity has been blocked.

text.text: The second is a direct effect of the potassium concentration itself.

Low and low-normal potassium is arrhythmogenic, 18 and in hypertensive, heart-failure and general populations the association between serum potassium and mortality is U-shaped, with its nadir between about 4.0 and 4.5 mmol/L. [12] [13] [14] [15] In experimental hypermineralocorticoid states cardiac fibrosis develops independently of potassium depletion, 19 so a potassium-mediated pathway is more plausibly electrophysiological than structural; it would operate whether or not the concentration was reached with supplementation.

text.text: The third is that achieved potassium marks disease severity rather than mediating risk.

Hypokalaemic PA is characterised by higher aldosterone, more suppressed renin and more target-organ damage than normokalaemic PA, 3 so patients whose potassium remains below 4.5 mmol/L under treatment may have more severe or less responsive disease.
Two observations bear on this.

The association was, if anything, stronger among patients normokalaemic at baseline (HR 0.57) than among those hypokalaemic at baseline (0.91), and it persisted among patients taking no potassium supplement, the group in which correction of hypokalaemia corresponds to the PAMO definition of biochemical response, 4 with no evidence of interaction by supplement use (Figure 3).

text.text: Both suggest that the prognostic information is carried by the concentration attained rather than only by the severity of the pre-treatment deficit or by how the concentration was reached-relevant to routine care, where about half of treated patients receive supplements-but these data cannot separate marker from mediator.

Finally, values of 5.0 mmol/L or more accompanied lower eGFR and more CKD and diabetes, and the crude estimate for that category moved from 1.21 to 0.80 with adjustment for renal function, so any upward limb is likely to reflect in part the renal impairment that both raises potassium and constrains MRA dosing, 20 rather than an effect of potassium itself.

text.text: Serum potassium in PA is treated as a safety parameter: it confirms that hypokalaemia has been corrected and that hyperkalaemia has not supervened.
If its prognostic information were exhausted by that role, the association would have disappeared once frankly hypokalaemic patients were excluded.

It did not: within 3.5 to <5.0 mmol/L, the 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L band carried a HR of 0.68 (95% CI, 0.53-0.88) for the composite outcome and 0.54 (0.36-0.83) for incident HF, and it was also lower than the adjacent 4.0-<4.5 mmol/L band (0.74 and 0.65).

text.text: What the data locate is a band inside the reference range, not a gradient, and the upper end is where the evidence stops.
This bears on how an adequate potassium response to medical treatment is defined.

The threshold of 3.6 mmol/L shared by the PAMO and PASO definitions was agreed by Delphi panels to classify whether hypokalaemia had been corrected, 4, 5 rather than derived from outcome data; the PASO investigators noted that their criteria could not be validated against hard endpoints. 5 In these data the threshold did not clearly separate patients by subsequent risk, and two features may explain this.

text.text: Whether the potassium criterion for an adequate response should be set higher cannot be established from an observational analysis, and the subgroup hypokalaemic at baseline was too small to exclude a difference, particularly for heart failure.
Outside PA the relationship between serum potassium and mortality is U-shaped, with both hypokalaemia and hyperkalaemia associated with excess mortality.

The category with lowest risk here matches that reported in a cohort of 21,334 patients with incident HF, where 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L was likewise the reference band. 13 The agreement is in which band carries the lowest risk, not in the shape of a curve, which these data do not resolve; the categories are wide and the formal shape tests were weak, so the correspondence should not be over-read.

text.text: Renin, followed in only a minority of patients here as elsewhere, is examined next.

Among 424 patients with plasma renin activity paired to potassium in the protocol windows, of whom 346 also met the criteria for the landmark modelling cohort, the change in potassium correlated weakly with the change in renin (Spearman rho, 0.15) and discriminated an unsuppressed renin at follow-up no better than chance (area under the curve, 0.523).

In an independent cohort of 155 patients on long-term medical therapy, 90% became normokalaemic, yet among the 57 with renin measured, classification of biochemical control by potassium and by renin agreed in only 49.1%. 17 A change in potassium therefore cannot be used as a proxy for renin status.

Nor can we claim that potassium carries information incremental to renin, since the two were never entered into a common model and the paired sample is too small to support that comparison.

text.text: Some limitations qualify these findings.
The case definition is administrative; the composite estimate was unchanged when restricted to codes specific to PA, but the heart-failure subsets were then too small to evaluate.

MRA dose, titration, adherence, supplement dose and dietary intake were unknown, so the achieved potassium may reflect treatment exposure as well as response to it, and interaction tests by supplement use had limited power.
The exposure is a single routine-care value; plasma and serum potassium differ systematically, which would preferentially affect the highest category.

The categories are 0.5 mmol/L wide, so these data identify the category with the lowest estimated risk, not the concentration at which risk is lowest, and the upward limb above 5.0 mmol/L is suggested rather than established.

The association varied by calendar period, which cannot be separated from follow-up duration; selection occurred in two steps and the weighted analysis is exploratory; the network is predominantly US-based.
Finally, the exposure is attained rather than assigned, so these estimates do not establish that altering potassium alters risk.

In adults with PA treated with an MRA, the potassium attained in the first six months was associated with subsequent cardiovascular risk and with incident HF with the lowest estimated risk in the 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L band, significantly lower than in either band below it.

text.text: That band lies inside the reference range, and the association was not attributable to the correction of frank hypokalaemia alone.
The band also lies well above the 3.6 mmol/L that consensus criteria accept as correction of hypokalaemia, so correction alone may be an insufficient treatment target.
Whether the early potassium response can serve as a treatment target, rather than a marker of risk, requires prospective evaluation.
Any such evaluation would need to compare titration strategies rather than attained concentrations, within the constraints that hyperkalaemia and renal function place on MRA dosing.

We searched PubMed from database inception to July 2026, without language restriction, for studies using the terms ("primary aldosteronism" OR hyperaldosteronism) AND ("mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist" OR spironolactone OR eplerenone) AND potassium AND (cardiovascular OR "heart failure" OR mortality).

Medically treated primary aldosteronism carries an excess of cardiovascular events over essential hypertension that is concentrated in patients whose renin remains suppressed, and a 2025 meta-analysis found unsuppressed post-treatment renin associated with fewer cardiovascular events.

The PAMO consensus defines a complete biochemical response as correction of hypokalaemia (a potassium of at least 3.6 mmol/L, set by expert agreement without outcome data) without supplementation together with normalisation of renin, and the 2025 Endocrine Society guideline recommends monitoring potassium and renin to guide titration, but neither specifies a potassium target.

Target ranges for serum potassium derive from hypertensive and heart-failure populations, in which the potassium-mortality association is U-shaped with a nadir near 4.0-4.5 mmol/L. We found no study relating the potassium concentration attained after MRA initiation to long-term cardiovascular outcomes in primary aldosteronism.

In 4,169 adults with primary aldosteronism in a multicentre electronic-health-record network, the potassium attained 14-180 days after MRA initiation was associated with myocardial infarction, stroke or death and with incident heart failure over a median of 3 years.

Estimated risk was lowest at 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L-about a third lower than at <4.0 mmol/L and a quarter lower than at 4.0-<4.5 mmol/L-a band inside the reference range; the association persisted after excluding frankly hypokalaemic values and among patients taking no potassium supplement, and a larger rise from baseline was associated with lower risk.

text.text: The change in potassium correlated only weakly with the change in renin, so potassium does not substitute for renin as a marker of treatment response.
The consensus threshold for correction of hypokalaemia, 3.6 mmol/L, did not separate patients by subsequent risk.

In MRA-treated primary aldosteronism, an achieved potassium below 4.5 mmol/L, including low-normal values, identifies patients at higher subsequent cardiovascular and heart-failure risk from a test already performed in nearly every treated patient.

Correction of hypokalaemia, the potassium criterion in current consensus definitions of treatment response, may therefore be an insufficient target, and that criterion merits reconsideration when those definitions are revised.
Because potassium and renin dissociate, both should be monitored, as current guidance recommends.

Whether titrating MRA therapy to reach 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L reduces risk, within the constraints that hyperkalaemia and renal function place on dosing, requires a prospective trial of a defined titration strategy.
